During a conversation on Figuring Out with Raj Shamani (@rajshamani ), Biocon founder Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw (@kiranmazumdar_shaw ) shared her perspective on why many talented people struggle with confidence. According to her, confidence isn't something people are born with or magically develop over time. Instead, she believes it grows from having clarity about your purpose, your direction, and the actions needed to achieve it.

👉🏼 Clarity Creates Confidence

Responding to a question about self-doubt, Kiran explained that confidence comes from being clear about what you want to achieve. When people have a strong sense of purpose and remain focused on executing that vision, they are less likely to second-guess themselves, even when challenges arise.

👉🏼 Uncertainty Fuels Self-Doubt

She added that constantly guessing, approximating, or hoping things will work out without a clear direction often leads to uncertainty. According to Kiran, when plans go wrong in the absence of clarity, self-doubt tends to grow much faster, making it harder to stay confident.

👉🏼 The Logical Indian's Perspective

Confidence isn't always about having all the answers. Developing a clear understanding of your goals, preparing thoughtfully, and taking consistent action can help reduce uncertainty and build greater confidence over time.

Do you think confidence comes first, or does it grow after finding clarity?

During a conversation on Figuring Out (@rajshamani ), Biocon founder Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw (@kiranmazumdar_shaw ), reflected on why she believes she has never struggled with self-doubt. Sharing her personal perspective, she said that having a strong sense of purpose has guided her decisions throughout her journey.

👉🏼 Purpose Over Self-Doubt

According to Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw, she has never experienced self-doubt because she has always been deeply driven by a clear purpose. She suggested that when people genuinely believe in the path they have chosen and the purpose behind their work, they may be less likely to question themselves.

👉🏼 Confidence Through Clarity

Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw believes that confidence grows from knowing why you're doing something rather than constantly seeking external validation. In her view, a meaningful purpose can provide the conviction needed to keep moving forward, even when faced with challenges.

👉🏼 The Logical Indian's Perspective

People experience self-doubt differently, and confidence can develop through a variety of experiences. While having a strong sense of purpose may help some people stay focused during challenges, others may build self-belief through learning, support, reflection, and gradual experience.

My mornings don’t change much. Same quiet 30 minutes before anyone needs anything from me. Same handful of decisions I don’t have to think about — what I eat, when I move, when the laptop opens and when it shuts. None of it photographs well. None of it would make an interesting reel on its own.

But here’s what I’ve noticed — the days that go well aren’t the days something exciting happens. They’re the days the boring stuff already happened, so I have the bandwidth left for whatever actually needs my full attention. A predictable routine isn’t the opposite of ambition. It’s what makes ambition sustainable past the first few months of adrenaline. 
  If your day feels chaotic, the fix probably isn’t a better morning routine video. It’s picking a handful of boring decisions and making them non-negotiable, so your energy stops leaking out through a hundred small choices you didn’t need to make in the first place.

Discipline isn’t dramatic. It’s just consistent. And consistent, it turns out, is the closest thing to a cheat code any of us actually get.

When my husband and co-founder, decided to put our savings into building a business almost everyone around us questioned the decision.

 Honestly, they had valid reasons too.

But we believed we had found a problem worth solving.

That’s what entrepreneurship is really about- 
having the conviction to follow an opportunity, while being smart enough to test that conviction with data.

Don’t let someone else’s fear become your limitation.

If you believe there’s a real problem worth solving
listen to yourself, validate it with data, and give yourself a chance to find out.

3. Listen to your consumers: Your audience will always show you where to grow next.

I keep saying this: for any regulated business, the biggest risk is regulatory risk. Today’s IRDAI draft on insurance commissions is a good reminder.

Broking is no different. A change in rules around retail F&O trading, how brokers can earn on client float, MTF requirements, or any of several other areas can change the economics of the business almost overnight.

So when valuing regulated businesses, you can’t just extrapolate current revenues and profits into the future. One regulation change can alter the economics, and the stock price along with it.

Pretty much everything in fintech comes with this risk 😬

People need to be able to close an account as easily as they open one, if not easier. Making it easy to open an account but impossible to close one is the oldest dark pattern in the book.

I think we are one of the few apps where the account closure option is clearly visible.

We (@zerodhaonline) close around 15,000 to 20,000 accounts every month for reasons ranging from company policies and trading losses to moving to another broker.

It might sound counterintuitive, but allowing customers to close their accounts easily is the mark of a good business.

The fancier a financial product looks, the bigger the catch usually is.

@prateek_learnapp and @zero1byzerodha do a nice job explaining this using leasing vs buying a car. A lower monthly payment can make leasing look like an obvious deal, but once you account for upfront costs, restrictions, and what you actually own at the end, the math looks very different.

I think this is true for most financial products. If it takes more than two sentences to explain how a product makes money and where the risk sits, you should probably stay away.

Boring is usually better.🙂

Bangalore produces around 7,000 tonnes of waste a day, roughly 3,000 tonnes of that is wet waste. All of it has to be collected, segregated, and processed every single day. A lot of it still ends up badly treated or in a landfill.

We got to know the @hasirudalainnovations team a few years ago. They’ve spent years doing the thankless part of this, collecting and segregating waste at scale. But wet waste has remained a problem. Dry waste has buyers. Wet waste goes bad too quickly to store, and composting it usually loses money.

@carbonlites takes that wet waste and turns it into biogas you can cook with. More importantly, they’ve made a business out of it.

Put the two together, and it’s fairly obvious. Hasiru Dala has the waste and knows how to sort it. Carbon Masters knows how to generate economic value out of it by generating biogas and organic manure. 

This problem goes beyond Bengaluru’s garbage. India imports about 60% of our LPG and half our natural gas. Turning our own waste into fuel is about as self-reliant as it gets. 

We need more people working on hard problems like this. That’s also why we’ve backed both Hasiru Dala Innovations and Carbon Masters through @rainmatterin.

We spent some time at their Harohalli plant to understand how it all fits together for our latest Rainmatter Original. If you’ve ever wondered where the waste from our homes actually goes, this is worth a watch (full episode link in bio and story).🙂

Back in 2010, one of the reasons we even considered becoming a brokerage firm was because of NSE NOW. It was a free trading platform provided by the @nseindia that brokers could offer to their clients.

While we were starting out, I had heard a lot of scary stories about the exchanges, but our experience was the total opposite. When we went to Chennai to inquire about a membership, they were incredibly welcoming. When they realised we didn’t have a lot of money, they even waived our membership fee of ~₹5 lakh. This is just one of many instances where the NSE was more than gracious throughout our journey.

In many ways, we are around only because of the NSE. When we started, we didn’t have the money to build our own trading platform. If there is one company I personally feel a sense of obligation towards, it is the NSE. 😀

Given that it is NSE, I have no doubt that it will be a successful IPO (PS: this is not a recommendation).

By the way, India’s market infrastructure and regulations are probably way ahead of most markets in the West. Exchanges here also act as the first-level regulators, which means a lot of what brokers traditionally do elsewhere is handled directly at the exchange and depository level. If it weren’t for that, I sometimes wonder what the point of brokers like us would even be. 😀

We were there as part of the CEO delegation with Hon’ble PM Modi, having dinner inside the Louvre of all places.

That’s Pavan next to me, cofounder of Skyroot Aerospace. Just another founder that night, another conversation, another photo under a French sky. Little did I know.

Right behind us in this pic, this massive Pegasus statue, a winged horse frozen mid flight, reaching for something bigger than gravity. Paris ka Pegasus toh symbol tha shayad. Kuch log sach mein udaan bharte hain.

In 2009, she spotted a gap in the Indian market—India lacked something as powerful as PayPal.
So, alongside Bipin Preet Singh, she launched MobiKwik—starting as a simple mobile recharge platform.

Fast forward to 2024:

✅ MobiKwik reported a ₹14.08 crore profit for FY24 (up from a ₹83.8 crore loss the previous year).

✅ Total income surged to ₹890 crore, and their IPO in December 2024 saw shares rise by 86% on the first day!

✅ Today, the company is valued at $474 million.

Upasana’s success shows that a woman entrepreneur from even a small town can build a startup that transforms industries.

Her journey is a masterclass in entrepreneurship, innovation, and leadership.

5 money rules my wife and I follow as a couple aged 45 with two kids.

1. We don’t spend money to look rich. 

We spend to become wealthy and gain freedom of our time.

So, there’s no car. It’s rented. 
We own the house we live in, no other real estate.

No spending on brands. No spending just to show off to people.

2. We spend extravagantly on high-quality food.

We know that what goes into our body is ultimately the biggest wealth we have, and unfortunately, healthy food is not cheap.

3. We spend on experiences more than things.

Things give you happiness once, and they have no end.

You remember experiences, and they make you a better person. 
You grow as a person.

We travelled 116 days last year!

4. We invest before spending.

As soon as our salary comes, the largest amount is invested.

The remaining amount is used for expenses.

We are recording this on the 30th. 
₹9,000 and ₹600 left in our bank accounts. 
Everything else is invested.

5. No budget for books and learning.

No amount of money spent is enough.

Ruchi is learning pottery, watercolor painting, and tennis.

Our kids also go to many classes.

These are our rules. 
They may not apply to you, but having your own rules is important in life.

Before you say yes to marriage, check these 5 things.

1. Why are you getting married? Is it for the sake of society? Is it for the sake of your parents? Is it for your own good?

2. How do you handle fights with your partner? Because fights will continue. If you handle them properly, then relationships will progress.

3. Do you have an alignment on money and responsibility? How will you spend money? How will you share responsibilities?

4. Do you have space for your own personality? You can make friends without involving their friends. You can live your own life without depending on them.

5. How will you spend your life after marriage? What are the expectations from your family? How will your daily routines be? What will be your living arrangements? What have you thought about your children?

This is an important decision. Don't take it in a hurry.

Suppose you have ₹100 and ₹10 of it goes missing.

No, right?

So when someone at the age of 24, 25, or 27 asks this question - “I’m not enjoying my career. But it’s too late. I won’t be able to change your career now.”

The person you find fascinating reads every day.

What relevant experience do you have?

As companies grow, the founder cannot be the source of every good idea. And probably should not be.

You need simple systems that allow curiosity to travel across teams, functions, and geographies.

For us, sometimes that is as basic as an open document, a few minutes every week, and one important rule: don’t judge an idea too quickly.

Innovation does not always need a complicated process.

Sometimes it just needs fewer barriers.

Ambition is rarely limited by the size of the goal. More often, it’s the small habits around it.

A little less discipline, a little more comparison, a little impatience, and even the biggest goal can remain just that: a goal.

Most ambitious goals don’t fail because they were too ambitious. They fail because the everyday habits needed to support them never quite show up.

Sometimes the best advice makes more sense when you read it backwards.

If you had asked me a few years ago how to win in life, I would have said work harder.

But my journey taught me something different.

Winning is not about being harsh, loud or ruthless. It’s about being clear, consistent and kind even when it’s hard.

It’s about understanding that no one is going to want your growth as much as you do. You have to show up for yourself every single day.

It’s about realizing that your title doesn’t define you, your work does. And if you make something with heart, it will always find its way to the right people.

I am still learning, still figuring it out. But these 5 things changed how I look at growth and life.

Sharing it here because I know someone out there needs to hear this today.
